en.title: Old universities
en.summary: The ancient universities of Britain and America, and the register of academic English.

paragraphs: The oldest universities in the English-speaking world have shaped science, law and government for centuries. In this lesson you will read about them and practise the complex noun phrases and formal structures typical of academic writing.

Teaching is recorded at Oxford from 1096, which makes it the oldest university in the English-speaking world, and Cambridge was founded in 1209 by scholars who had left Oxford after a dispute with townspeople. St Andrews in Scotland dates from 1413. Across the Atlantic, Harvard was founded in 1636 to train ministers, and Yale in 1701. Both Oxford and Cambridge are made up of independent colleges, in which students live, eat and receive small-group teaching, known as tutorials in Oxford and supervisions in Cambridge. For centuries these institutions admitted only men from privileged families; women were first allowed to take degrees at Oxford in 1920 and at Cambridge, in the full sense, only in 1948.
**1. Complex noun phrases pack information before the noun.** Academic writing prefers a long noun phrase to a string of short sentences. See Introduction to Grammar: Substantives (nouns).

paragraphs: **2. Formal subordination.** Whereby, in which, and by which join clauses in formal writing. See Introduction to Grammar: Relative clauses.

items: **Fellow** is a senior member of a college; **undergraduate** and **postgraduate** are student levels.
**Alma mater** is Latin for the university you attended.

paragraphs: The Oxford and Cambridge Boat Race has been held on the Thames since 1829, and it is watched by hundreds of thousands of people along the river.
